items.prompt: White is in check from the black rook. Tap every square the white king can step to, to get out of check.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king can move to.
The rook attacks e2 along the file.

hints: The rook attacks every square on its file, all the way down to the king.
A king cannot step onto a square the enemy attacks, and moving along the file stays in line with the rook.
Step sideways, off the e-file. Check each of the four sideways squares.
items.explain: The rook attacks the whole e-file, so the king cannot go to e2. It can step off the file to d1, d2, f1 or f2, where no black piece attacks it.

items.prompt: White is in check. Get out of check without moving the king: block the rook's line or capture it.

claims.statement: The white rook can capture the checking rook.
The bishop can block on e2.
The bishop can block on e6.
A bishop move that does not stop the check is not allowed.

hints: There are three ways out of check: move the king, block, or capture the checking piece. You are asked for the other two.
Which white piece can reach the e-file between the rooks? Which can take the black rook?
The white rook on a8 sees the black rook along the eighth rank, and the bishop can reach e2 or e6.
items.explain: The white rook on a8 can capture the black rook, or the bishop can step in front of the king, on e2 or e6. Any other move leaves the king in check, so it is not allowed.

items.prompt: A black knight gives check. Can White get out of check by putting a piece between the knight and the king? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: White's only legal moves are two captures of the knight and three king moves.

hints: Think about how a knight attacks: does it travel along a line?
Look at the list of replies the game allows. Are there any that put a piece between?
items.explain: A knight jumps straight to its target, so there is no line to block. White's only legal replies are to capture the knight (queen or pawn) or move the king.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?
hints: Is Black's king attacked right now?
If it is, look for a way out: a king move, a block, or a capture.
The king's own pawns stand on the three squares in front of it.
items.explain: The rook attacks the king along the back rank. The king has no safe square (its own pawns block three squares and the rook covers the others), and Black has nothing to block or capture with. That is checkmate.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?

claims.statement: Black is in check but not checkmated.
Black has exactly one legal move: Kf7.

hints: Is Black's king attacked right now?
If it is, does the king have any way out?
A pawn that is missing from the king's shelter can leave a square free.
items.explain: The king is in check, but the pawn that used to stand on f7 is gone, so the king can step to f7. It is check, not checkmate.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?
hints: Is Black's king attacked right now?
The white queen is on the eighth rank, the same rank as the king.
Which squares could the king step to? Check the white king as well as the queen.
items.explain: The queen attacks the king along the eighth rank. The white king covers g7 and h7, and the queen covers g8, so there is nowhere to go and nothing to capture or block. Checkmate.

items.prompt: Black to move. The queen is one square lower than before. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?
hints: Is Black's king attacked right now?
Count the squares the king could move to. Are any safe?
Black's king has no safe square, and it is not attacked.
items.explain: Black is not in check, because the queen on f7 does not attack h8, but every square the king could go to is covered. A player with no legal move who is not in check is stalemated: the game is a draw.

items.prompt: White to move. Find checkmate. Be careful: some queen moves leave Black with no move at all.
hints: Where is Black's king? Which squares around it does White's king already cover?
You want to give check, and leave the king no square. Beware of quiet moves that take away its last square without giving check.
The queen belongs on the eighth rank.
items.explain: Qf8 gives check along the eighth rank, and the king has no square: checkmate. Qf7 (and Qc4) take away the king's last squares without giving check, and that is stalemate: a draw instead of a win.

feedback_by_move.f1f7: Stalemate: Black has no legal move and is not in check, so the game is a draw (see the previous pair of positions).

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?
hints: Is the black king attacked?
If not, can it move anywhere safe?
items.explain: The king on a8 is not attacked, but the queen and the white king cover a7, b7 and b8. No legal move and no check: stalemate.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?
hints: Is the black king attacked?
Could the king take the queen? Look at what protects her.
items.explain: The queen attacks the king and the white king protects the queen, so the black king cannot capture her. It has no other square: checkmate.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?

claims.statement: Black is in check but has legal moves.
The king can step to these squares.

hints: Is the black king attacked?
A knight's check cannot be blocked. Can the king step away?
items.explain: The knight on g6 attacks h8, so Black is in check, but the king can step away to g8, g7 or h7. It is check, not checkmate.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is this check, checkmate, stalemate, or none of these?

claims.statement: Black is not in check and has legal moves.

hints: Is the black king attacked?
Does Black have any legal move?
items.explain: The king is not attacked and it can move, so the game simply goes on.

items.prompt: Castle kingside.
hints: Castling is a king move. Which way is kingside, toward the h-file?
The king moves two squares toward the rook.
Move the king from e1 to g1; the rook follows.
items.explain: The king goes two squares toward the rook on h1, to g1, and the rook jumps to f1. Everything between the king and the rook is empty, and the king has never moved.

items.prompt: Only a white king and rook stand on their starting squares, with nothing in between. Can White castle kingside? Predict, then check.
hints: Have the king and rook moved? Are the squares between them empty?
Does any black piece attack the squares the king passes over and lands on?
items.explain: All four conditions are met: the king and the rook have not moved, f1 and g1 are empty, the king is not in check, and nothing attacks f1 or g1.

items.prompt: A black rook stands on f3. Can White castle kingside? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The black rook attacks f1, the square the king would pass over.

hints: Castling moves the king across the square next to it. Which square is that here?
Does any black piece attack that square?
The rook on f3 looks down the f-file at f1.
items.explain: The king would pass over f1 on its way to g1, and the rook on f3 attacks f1. The king may not cross an attacked square, so castling is not allowed here.

items.prompt: A black rook stands on b8 and attacks b1. Can White castle queenside? Predict, then check.
hints: Which squares does the king pass over and land on? It goes e1, d1, c1.
Is b1 one of them? Only the rook crosses b1.
Check whether d1 and c1 are attacked.
items.explain: The king only travels over d1 and lands on c1, and neither is attacked. The rook crosses b1, but only the king's squares have to be safe, so White can castle.

items.prompt: A black rook gives check along the e-file. Can White castle? Predict, then check.
hints: Is White's king attacked right now?
You must get out of check, and castling is not one of the three ways.
items.explain: You cannot castle out of check. The king must move, or the check must be blocked or captured.

items.prompt: White's king moved earlier in this game and has come back to e1. Both rooks are on their squares and the squares between are empty. Can White castle? Predict, then check.
hints: Castling needs the king and the rook to have never moved.
Did White's king ever move?
items.explain: Once the king has moved, castling is gone for the rest of the game, even if the king comes home. The same is true of a rook that has moved: that side is lost.

items.prompt: White wants to castle. Which castling move can White play here?
hints: Check each side: the squares between the king and the rook must be empty.
Look at b1, c1 and d1.
items.explain: The knight on b1 stands between the king and the queenside rook, so only kingside castling is possible.

items.prompt: Black has just played the pawn from d7 to d5, next to your pawn. Capture it en passant.

claims.statement: White can capture en passant on d6.
White can also simply push the pawn.

hints: The black pawn jumped two squares and landed right beside your pawn.
You capture it as if it had moved only one square. Which square is that?
Your pawn goes diagonally to d6, and the black pawn on d5 disappears.
items.explain: The black pawn jumped from d7 to d5 and now stands beside the pawn on e5. White may capture it as if it had stopped on d6: the pawn moves e5 to d6 and the pawn on d5 is removed.

feedback_by_move.e5e6: That is an ordinary pawn move. The en passant capture goes to d6.

items.prompt: Black has just played d7-d5. Can White capture that pawn en passant? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The capture on d6 is legal.

hints: Did the black pawn just jump two squares?
Is it right beside White's pawn?
items.explain: The pawn has just jumped two squares and landed beside White's pawn, so en passant is available now.

items.prompt: The same pawns, but Black's pawn reached d5 two moves ago and White played something else since. Can White capture it en passant now? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The capture on d6 is not legal now.
White's pawn can still move forward.

hints: En passant is only possible straight after the two-square jump.
Was the jump the last move?
items.explain: En passant must be played at once. If White waits a move, the chance is gone for good.

items.prompt: White wants to promote the pawn on e7. Find the best way to do it.

claims.statement: Capturing on d8 and promoting to a queen is the engine's best move.
Promoting on e8 loses the new queen.

hints: A pawn can promote straight ahead or by capturing diagonally. Which promotion squares are there?
Check each promotion square: does an enemy piece attack it?
The rook on d8 attacks e8 but can be captured.
items.explain: The rook on d8 covers e8, so a queen made there would be captured. Capturing the rook on d8 promotes and wins a rook at the same time.

feedback_by_move.e7e8q: The black rook on d8 captures the new queen.

items.prompt: White has a king and a rook. Black has only a king. Can White force checkmate? Predict, then check.
hints: Think about which pieces can drive a king into a corner.
A rook controls a whole line.
items.explain: A king and a rook can force checkmate against a bare king. It takes some technique, which you will practise soon.

items.prompt: White has a king and a knight. Black has only a king. Can White force checkmate? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: With best play from both sides the game is a draw.
The engine sees the position as equal.

hints: A rook can win. Is a knight just as strong in an ending with nothing else on the board?
A knight and a king cannot trap a lone king in a corner.
items.explain: A king and a single knight cannot force checkmate, and neither can a king and a single bishop. The game is a draw even though White has an extra piece: when there are not enough pieces left to checkmate, the game is a draw.

items.prompt: White to move. Which special move is available? (Castling, en passant, promotion, or none of these.)

claims.statement: All of White's legal moves; none is an en passant capture or a promotion.

hints: Look at the kings and the rooks.
Are there any pawns at all?
items.explain: The king and both rooks are on their starting squares with empty squares between, so castling is possible. There are no pawns, so no en passant and no promotion.

items.prompt: Black to move. White has just played e2-e4. Which special move is available? (Castling, en passant, promotion, or none of these.)

claims.statement: Black can capture en passant on e3.

hints: Which pawn just jumped two squares?
Is there a black pawn beside it?
items.explain: The white pawn has just jumped two squares and stands beside the black pawn on d4, so Black can capture it en passant, landing on e3. There are no rooks to castle with and no pawn near the last rank.

items.prompt: White to move. Which special move is available? (Castling, en passant, promotion, or none of these.)
hints: Look at the pawns.
How far is the white pawn from the last rank?
items.explain: The pawn on a7 is one step from the last rank, so it can promote. The kings have no rooks to castle with, and no black pawn can be captured en passant.

items.prompt: White to move. Which special move is available? (Castling, en passant, promotion, or none of these.)

claims.statement: White's legal moves are only king moves.

hints: Are there any rooks?
Did a pawn just jump two squares? Is any pawn near the last rank?
items.explain: There are no rooks and the pawns face each other, so there is nothing to castle with, nothing to take en passant and nothing to promote. White's only legal moves are king moves.
